NFL Draft Position Futures: Racing to the No. 1 Pick

Published November 18, 2026 · 9 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

By mid-November, a handful of NFL teams have stopped pretending. The playoff math is dead, the trade deadline has passed, and the only scoreboard that still matters for a 2-9 roster is the one that runs in reverse: strength of schedule, remaining opponents, and where a loss this Sunday lands you on draft day in April. Sportsbooks noticed this a long time ago, and most major books now post a running market on exactly that outcome — not who wins the Super Bowl, but who picks first. It's a smaller, stranger corner of the futures board, and it's priced almost nothing like the markets bettors are used to.

  2. How sportsbooks build the number

What a draft-position future actually is

A draft-position future asks a single question: which team will own the first overall pick in next April's draft, or, in a wider version of the market, which teams will finish in the top three, top five, or bottom of the league. It's structurally the same bet as a championship future — odds posted on every eligible team, adjusted as the season plays out — just pointed at the opposite end of the standings. Books typically open this market around midseason, once enough results exist to separate the genuinely bad teams from the merely unlucky ones, and keep it live through the final week of the regular season.

It's worth being precise about terminology here: this is a future on draft position, not a bet on which prospect a team will actually select. A handful of operators also run separate, much smaller markets on which player goes first overall, but that's a different product with its own information problems — scouting reports, pre-draft testing, team-specific needs — and isn't what most bettors mean when they talk about "tanking" futures.

How sportsbooks build the number

The starting input is simply the current standings, inverted. A team sitting at 2-9 with six games left is the early favorite for the No. 1 pick in the same mechanical sense a 10-1 team is the Super Bowl favorite — fewest wins, most losses, most team-controlled losing left to do. From there, a trading desk layers in remaining schedule strength, since a bad team with five winnable games left is a weaker bet for the top pick than an equally bad team facing five other losing teams. Coaching staff job security matters too: a team with its coach already fired or clearly playing out the string tends to get a small bump toward "worse," since there's less reason to expect a late-season turnaround built on desperation.

Because the sample of bettors interested in this market is small and the information is mostly public record, the vig tends to be wider than on mainstream markets like a spread or total — books aren't worried about getting run over by sharp money here the way they are on a Sunday spread, so there's less competitive pressure to trim the number down.

Why the strength-of-schedule tiebreaker matters more than record

This is the detail that trips up casual bettors on this market. The NFL's actual draft order isn't settled by raw win total alone — ties at the bottom of the standings are broken using strength of schedule, with the team that faced the easier opponents getting the worse tiebreaker (and therefore the better draft slot) when records match. That means two 3-14 teams can land picks a full slot apart purely because one of them played a softer slate, with nothing either front office did differently. A sportsbook's number has to account for this, which is why you'll sometimes see a team with a marginally better record still priced as the favorite for the No. 1 pick over a team with an identical or worse one — the schedule-strength math is already baked in.

The incentive problem these markets create

The existence of a visible, bettable "race to the bottom" number is itself a little uncomfortable for a league that otherwise spends enormous effort protecting competitive integrity, and it's worth being upfront about why. Once a fan base, a front office, and now a betting market all have the same rooting interest — lose, but lose in a way that doesn't look like losing on purpose — the incentive to actually play hard in Week 15 gets murkier. The league office has never sanctioned a team for simply having a bad roster, and nothing about posting a betting line changes that; the exposure is reputational, not competitive, since nobody is wagering on the outcome of an individual snap the way they might on a point spread. Still, it's a fair thing to have in the back of your mind reading a late-season box score from a team that's clearly out of it.

Takeaway: A draft-position future is priced off the same inverted logic as a championship future, but with a thinner market, a wider vig, and one extra layer regular bettors miss: the strength-of-schedule tiebreaker that decides ties at the bottom of the standings, not just the win column.

What actually moves the number week to week

Three things move this market more than anything else. A quarterback change, especially a rookie or backup getting extended run, can swing the number hard in either direction depending on how that player looks — a surprisingly competent fill-in can tank a team's draft odds by winning games nobody expected. A coaching change, whether a midseason firing or a lame-duck staff coasting to the offseason, tends to nudge the number toward "worse," since interim staffs have historically been more willing to manage snap counts and rest veterans once the season is clearly over. And divisional matchups against other bad teams create the market's most volatile swings, since two teams both trying to lose still have to play each other, and only one of them can.

What to know before betting one

If you're considering a draft-position future, treat it the way you'd treat any other long-shot futures bet: size it small, expect the number to be wider than you're used to seeing on a spread, and don't assume the team with the worse record today is locked into the better pick, since the schedule-strength tiebreaker can flip that late. It's also worth checking a second book before betting, since thin markets like this one are exactly where you'll find the biggest pricing gaps between operators — see our guide on line shopping across sportsbooks for why that gap tends to be larger on lower-volume markets than on a mainstream spread or total.

Frequently asked questions

When do sportsbooks typically open draft-position futures?

Most major books post the market around the midpoint of the season, once there's enough of a sample to separate teams that are genuinely struggling from teams that just had a rough stretch. Some operators keep a lighter version of it running from the preseason, but it carries little weight until real results exist.

Does a team's record alone decide who's favored for the No. 1 pick?

No. The NFL breaks ties among teams with the same record using strength of schedule, with the team that faced easier opponents getting the better draft slot. A sportsbook's number accounts for this, so the favorite isn't always the team with the single worst record at a given moment.

Is betting on draft position the same as betting on which player gets picked?

No — those are separate markets. A draft-position future is about which team ends up with a given pick. A handful of operators separately offer much thinner markets on which specific prospect goes first overall, which depends on scouting and team needs rather than standings.

Why is the vig wider on this market than on a typical NFL spread?

Betting volume is much lower, so sportsbooks don't face the same competitive pressure from sharp bettors to tighten the price. With less action to balance, books can carry a wider margin without much risk of being exploited at scale.

What single event moves this market the most during the season?

A change at quarterback is usually the biggest driver, since a bad team that starts winning unexpectedly with a backup or rookie can shift its draft odds sharply. Coaching changes and head-to-head matchups between two struggling teams also produce noticeable swings.
